opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think throughput is really the metric that matters if you care about robots actually being useful in the real world. For a long time in robot learning, the standard metric was success rate: you set up a task, you run the policy, say, twenty times, and you count how many times it succeeds. That's fine for research, but it hides a lot of what matters in deployment.

Think about a real job, like folding laundry, assembling boxes, or making espresso. Nobody pays for a robot that eventually succeeds. What matters is how many shirts it folds per hour, how many boxes per hour. Throughput captures speed and reliability together. If a policy succeeds 95% of the time but is very slow and hesitant, or it makes a mistake and takes forever to recover, that shows up in throughput. If it retries a lot, that shows up too. So it's a much more honest number.

For Pi 0.6*, this was especially important because the whole point of that work was learning from experience, using reinforcement learning on real-world data, including autonomous rollouts and human corrections. Imitation learning on demonstrations can get you to a reasonable success rate, but the policy tends to be bounded by the demonstrations: it's often slower, it hesitates, and small errors compound. When you train with RL against a value function, the model learns to do the task faster and more robustly. Success rate alone wouldn't show that; you might already be near the ceiling. But throughput showed a big jump, in some tasks more than doubling.

The other thing I like about throughput is that it naturally rewards recovery. In long-horizon tasks like folding a varied pile of laundry, things go wrong all the time. A good policy isn't one that never makes mistakes; it's one that notices and fixes them quickly. Throughput measures that directly.

And practically, it lets us run the robot for hours, like a whole day making coffee or folding boxes, and that's what convinces us, and hopefully other people, that this is getting close to something deployable rather than just a demo.

r001.rationale: It describes throughput as how many items the robot completes per hour, such as shirts or boxes, which communicates successful work completed within a fixed time.

r002.rationale: It discusses mistakes and recovery, but does not identify whether the robot performed the task humans intended as an open research problem.

r003.rationale: It mentions throughput more than doubling on some tasks, but does not state that Pi 0.6* beat the best human data collectors’ baseline on clothes folding.

fable-5.1.text:
Guest: Because throughput is the number that actually matters once you move out of the demo setting and into real deployment. For a long time the field has reported success rate, and success rate is useful, but it hides two things. First, it hides how long the robot takes. A policy that succeeds 90 percent of the time but needs three attempts and a lot of hesitation to get there is not the same as one that succeeds 90 percent of the time cleanly. Second, it hides what happens after failure. If the robot drops a cup, does it recover and keep going, or does it freeze and wait for a human? Throughput captures both, because it is simply: how much useful work gets done per unit of time, including the slow attempts and the recoveries.

In Pi 0.6*, the thing we were really trying to show is that the RL step, the Recap stage, does not just make the policy a little more accurate on a held-out eval. It makes the robot faster and more robust over long runs, hours of making espresso drinks, folding laundry, assembling boxes. Those are tasks where the baseline model could technically do the task, but it was slow and brittle. When you plot throughput, you see roughly a doubling, and about half of the failures going away, and that is a number a business can actually reason about. A coffee shop does not care about success rate in isolation. It cares how many drinks per hour the robot can serve.

I would also say throughput keeps us honest. It is very easy to cherry-pick episodes or reset the scene between trials. If you commit to measuring how much gets done over a long, continuous stretch with no human intervention, you have to confront everything, the edge cases, the slow modes, the compounding errors. So it is both a better metric for users and a stricter metric for us as researchers.

r001.rationale: It defines throughput as “how much useful work gets done per unit of time,” which conveys completed work measured over time.

r002.rationale: It does not identify determining whether the robot performs the task humans intended as an open research problem.

r003.rationale: It does not say Pi 0.6* exceeded the best human data collectors’ baseline on clothes folding.

astra-6.text:
I think throughput is useful because it asks a practical question: how much useful work does the robot actually get done in a given amount of time? Success rate alone doesn’t capture that. A robot might succeed very reliably but take a long time on every attempt. And speed alone isn’t enough either, because moving quickly doesn’t help if it keeps failing.

So, for Pi 0.6*, looking at successfully completed tasks per unit of time brings those two dimensions together. It also makes the cost of retries and recovery visible. You still want to look at task quality and safety separately, but throughput gives you a useful measure of whether better robot behavior translates into more useful work.

r001.rationale: It describes throughput as successfully completed tasks per unit of time.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss whether the robot performs the task humans intended as an open research problem.

r003.rationale: It makes no claim about Pi 0.6* surpassing human data collectors on clothes folding.

sol-6.1.text: I think throughput is useful because it asks a very practical question: how much useful work does the robot actually get done over time? A robot might succeed on a task, but if it takes a long time or needs frequent human intervention, that success alone doesn’t tell you how productive it is. Throughput brings speed, reliability, and recovery into the same picture. For Pi 0.6*, it’s a way to evaluate whether improvements translate into more completed work, rather than just better performance on an isolated attempt.

r001.rationale: It describes throughput as how much useful work the robot gets done over time, including completed work, which conveys successful work per time interval.
